Figure - DSpace Home Page 5.3 Single-Sign On Procedure By default new users of DSpace are forced to register, even if they already have a UQU network ID. DSpace then copies the user’s credentials locally into a PostgreSQL database. UQU’s requirements required a transparent login procedure. The solution implemented forced DSpace to accept any user who already existed in UQU’s eDirectory - which is part of a Novell Directory Service (NDS) directory database. In order to achieve this, we had to overcome a number of technical obstacles: DSpace does not support the NDS authentication method. DSpace versions prior to 1.3 do not support the LDAP authentication method which is 100% compatible with NDS. We had already installed version 1.2 as it was the latest and most stable version at the time of implementation. We circumvented these challenges by installing the DSpace LDAP support module and modified dspace.conf file from DSpace version 1.3.0. Further we reconfigured the file web.xml "the main file controlling the appearance of any DSpace html form field" so that it would complement the modifications. The system is now configured such that when an existing UQU user logs in, the user’s credentials are read from the LDAP server (which is a NOVELL eDirectory or NDS server). Hence the user automatically has browsing permission granted. DSpace administrator can grant additional access privileges as needed. These are simply recommendations based on MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) setup; since DSpace is built on open source, standards-based tools, there are numerous other possibilities and setups. UNIX-like OS (Linux, HP/UX etc) We freely downloaded and installed RedHat enterprise server 3.0 with the latest patches and fixes (Linux kernel 2.6.9-5.ELsmp #1 SMP i686 i386 GNU/Linux). The machine we used for this installation was an HP Proliant ML370 Intel Xeon 3.4 processor, with 2x72 GB HDs, and 3GB Memory. Java 1.4 or later (standard SDK is fine, no need for J2EE) The JDK (1_5_0_03) had already been downloaded from Sun and installed in /usr/jdk1.5.0_03. Apache Ant 1.5 or later (Java make-like tool) Apache-ant-1.6.3 was downloaded and installed. We installed it as root user in the directory /usr/local as follows: cd /usr/local tar -xzvf apache*.tar.gz mv apache-ant-1.6.3 ant PostgreSQL 7.3 or later, an open source relational database For our fortune, we installed PostgreSQL 8.0, it was more stable and has lots of new features that beneficial to UQU requirements. To meet the UQU settings we compiled PostgreSQL with the following options to the 'configure' script: --enable-multibyte --enable-unicode --with-java We tighten up security a bit by editing pg_hba.conf and adding this line: host dspace dspace 127.0.0.1 255.255.255.255 md5 Then we had to restart PostgreSQL. Jakarta Tomcat 4.x/5.x or equivalent, such as Jetty or Caucho Resin. jakarta-tomcat-5.5.9 was downloaded and installed. We already know that DSpace will need to run as the same user as Tomcat, so we installed and run Tomcat as a user called 'dspace'. Also we previously warned that we need to ensure that Tomcat has; a) enough memory to run DSpace and, b) uses UTF-8 as its default file encoding for international character support. So made sure that in our startup scripts (etc) that the following environment variable is set: JAVA_OPTS="-Xmx512M -Xms64M -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8" The next step was to create a user dspace with home directory /home/dspace. As user dspace we then proceeded to download and installed Tomcat (5.5.9) in /home/dspace as follows: cd /home/dspace tar -xzvf jakarta-tomcat-5.5.9.tar.gz mv jakarta-tomcat-5.5.9 tomcat The following paths were set up in /etc/profile: LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/pgsql/lib export LD_LIBRARY_PATH PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/pgsql/bin export JAVA_HOME=/usr/jdk1.5.0_03 export CATALINA_HOME=/home/dspace/tomcat export ANT_HOME=/usr/local/ant export PATH=${PATH}:${ANT_HOME}/bin export PATH=${PATH}:${JAVA_HOME}/jre/bin As user dspace we started Tomcat from the /home/dspace/tomcat/bin directory using the following command: -bash-3.00$ /home/dspace/tomcat/bin/startup.sh Using CATALINA_BASE: /home/dspace/tomcat Using CATALINA_HOME: /home/dspace/tomcat Using CATALINA_TMPDIR: /home/dspace/tomcat/temp Using JRE_HOME: /usr/jdk1.5.0_03 Running nmap on the IP address of the machine confirmed that Tomcat was running and listening for connections on port 8080: -bash-3.00$ nmap

user dspace we started Tomcat from the /home/dspace/tomcat/bin directory using the following command: -bash-3.00$ /home/dspace/tomcat/bin/startup.sh Using CATALINA_BASE: /home/dspace/tomcat Using CATALINA_HOME: /home/dspace/tomcat Using CATALINA_TMPDIR: /home/dspace/tomcat/temp Using JRE_HOME: /usr/jdk1.5.0_03 Running nmap on the IP address of the machine confirmed that Tomcat was running and listening for connections on port 8080: -bash-3.00$ nmap 212.26.17.30 (this IP is our dspace.uqu.edu.sa server) Starting nmap 3.70 ( http://www.insecure.org/nmap/ ) at 2005-12-08 13:56 AST Interesting ports on dspace.uqu.edu.sa (212.26.17.30): (The 1655 ports scanned but not shown below are in state: closed) PORT STATE SERVICE 22/tcp open ssh 111/tcp open rpcbind 5432/tcp open postgres 8009/tcp open ajp13 8080/tcp open http-proxy Nmap run completed -- 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 0.183 seconds As user dspace we then downloaded DSpace (1.2.2) and installed it in the home directory of the dspace user /home/dspace as follows: cd /home/dspace gunzip -c dspace-1.2.2-source.tar.gz | tar -xf - The next task as user dspace was to download the postgresql-8.0-311.jdbc3.jar file which was specific to the version of the JDK (1.5.0) and the version of PostgreSQL (8.0). The next task was getting PostgreSQL working. PostgreSQL (8.0.1) was already installed. The first step was to become user postgres from a root login by using the command: su - postgres The postgres user has administrative control over PostgreSQL and commands typed by this user can be used to administer the database directly. The first step was to create a new Postgres database installation using the following command: initdb -D /var/lib/pgsql/data The next step was to edit the file /var/lib/pgsql/data/pg_hba.conf and add the following lines: We have to add this line – otherwise we will get the following error: [createdb: could not connect to database template1: FATAL: IDENT authentication failed for user "dspace"] host all all 127.0.0.1 255.255.255.255 trust host dspace dspace 127.0.0.1 255.255.255.255 md5 local template1 postgres trust local template1 dspace trust I then had to become root and start PostgreSQL as follows: [root@cd data]# /usr/local/pgsql/bin/pg_ctl -D /usr/local/pgsql/data -l /tmp/pgsql.log start Starting postgresql service: [ OK ] It was then necessary to su - postgres and create the user dspace and the database dspace as follows: -bash-3.00$ createuser -U postgres -d -A -P dspace Enter password for new user: Enter it again: CREATE USER -bash-3.00$ createdb -U dspace -E UNICODE dspace CREATE DATABASE As user dspace it was then necessary to edit the file /home/dspace/config/dspace.cfg and add the appropriate entries, paying particular attention to changing all the paths from /dspace/ to /home/dspace/ Before running ant to build dspace it was necessary to remove a number of rpm's that had been installed as part of the default Fedora Core 3 upgrade of everything: [root@cd ~]# rpm -e --nodeps libgcj gcc-java libgcj-devel gettext ant tomcat (If this is not done you will get cryptic error messages such as: BUILD FAILED file:/home/dspace/dspace-1.2.1-source/build.xml:109: Error running gcj34 compiler) As user dspace the application was now successfully built using the commands: [dspace@cd dspace-1.2.1-source]$ ant [dspace@cd dspace-1.2.1-source]$ ant fresh_install We successfully copied over the .war files to tomcat webapps directory as

this is not done you will get cryptic error messages such as: BUILD FAILED file:/home/dspace/dspace-1.2.1-source/build.xml:109: Error running gcj34 compiler) As user dspace the application was now successfully built using the commands: [dspace@cd dspace-1.2.1-source]$ ant [dspace@cd dspace-1.2.1-source]$ ant fresh_install We successfully copied over the .war files to tomcat webapps directory as shown below and DSpace ran cd /home/dspace/dspace-1.2.1-source/build/ cp *.war /home/dspace/tomcat/webapps We ran the following script to set up the administrator account: /home/dspace/bin/create-administrator. For administrative purposes I created the following cron tasks: su - postgres -bash-3.00$ crontab -l # Clean up the database nightly at 2.40am 40 2 * * * vacuumdb --analyze dspace > /dev/null 2>&1 su - dspace [dspace@cd ~]$ crontab -l 0 1 * * * /home/dspace/bin/sub-daily # Run the media filter at 02:00 every day 0 2 * * * /home/dspace/bin/filter-media Conclusion: Overall the installation of DSpace was straightforward. Minor errors in the official documentation were easily spotted and had straightforward solutions. DSpace is sufficiently flexible for the system administrators to allow researchers who wish to collaborate on a particular submission a policy to do so, although there is no particular collaborative workspace functionality.
